title: What it was like dancing with Duke Ellington
summary: Green calls it the greatest experience; he recalls the Mao Brothers, Snake-Hips Tucker numbers, Ellington inheriting the Cotton Pickers, and Ellington's stature with visiting royalty.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: So, what was it like dancing with Duke?

Oh, I guess -- I don't know if it was ever explained, but I think it's the greatest think anyone could have experienced because -- it was all truth, I would say. Anyone who wanted to be anything for theirself or the audiences, see -- see, fan clubs were very popular, see. They were also discovering acts, you know. And you would get invited away from your appearance into theirs, see.
Did a white dancer ever dance with the Duke, that you know of?
No, I don't think so -- quite sure.
His music's so progressive, you have to be a great dancer.
Well, those brothers -- the Mayo Brothers --
Uh-huh. Eddie Mao and his brother.

Yes. There was Mizzie Nizz and they was featuring a song in the called 'Pappa De Da Da' and Chuck and Chuckles -- they was doing scattin' at the Kit Kat. Now, these was Duke Ellington's works (unintelligible) Rocking in Rhythm by 'Snake-Hips' Tucker -- that was Duke Ellington's music. They were all originals.
You were dancing to all the different music?

MR. GREEN: Well, there are different dancers, see. There were other dancers on the show with Duke Ellington at that time. It was his tour, see. This is the days of the big band era, you see. Just arriving, but I mean he was a big band before the big band era because he was with McKinney's Cotton Pickers, you see. And he inherited that orchestra, see, which became Duke Ellington and his Orchestra, you see. Especially then, and he was always in great demand because he was -- I think

they would call him the forager of that instrument which is known as piano, you know. He eventually said that the pianist walks in -- comes in and steals the show, see. He had sayings, he was very educational everywhere he was at, you see. He was a gourmet and all this. People had to be very diplomatic, you know, and on their toes at all times, because the most important people in the world used to try to visit Duke Ellington. Kings would walk back stage or rise up in the audience and say -- ask a question, you know. That's how important he was. And in this country, how can they explain America (unintelligible) you know, as land of the free and so on, you see. Yeah, by the way, Harry Richmond -- he was in the show. He was on the tour. See, that's -- now, he was a star, you can understand this, see. But the bands liked to be up on stage. They had moved from down in the audience -- the pit. They became -- you know, on-stage bands, and that's what he was -- I think he was number one man. He was the number one that -- on-stage bands.
